p.span: ON APPEAL FROM THE CROWN COURT AT STOKE ON TRENT
B e f o r e:
Sitting as a Judge of the Court of Appeal Criminal Division
Computer Aided Transcription of Epiq Europe Ltd,
Lower Ground Floor, 46 Chancery Lane, London WC2A 1JE
Tel No: 020 7404 1400; Email: rcj@epiqglobal.co.uk (Official Shorthand Writers to the Court)
appeared on behalf of the Appellant
J U D G M E N T

content.p: On 22 October 2025, in the Crown Court at Stoke on Trent, the appellant was sentenced by His Honour Judge McConaghy to 27 months' imprisonment for an offence of violent disorder, contrary to section 2 of the Public Order Act 1986.
The appellant now appeals against sentence with the leave of the single judge.

The disorder took place in the immediate aftermath of the stabbings in Southport at the end of July 2024 which caused widespread unrest across the country fuelled by misinformation about the ethnicity and immigration status of the offender.

On the afternoon of 3 August 2024 there were protests in the Hanley area of Stoke on Trent with rival factions of Asian groups and far right groups. There were multiple attacks and fights between rival groups which managed to confront each other at various locations away from the main police cordon, where police in riot gear were deployed. The disorder as a whole involved some 300 people and lasted a number of hours. Projectiles were thrown causing damage to premises and to street furniture. There were injuries to police officers and to members of the public. Extremist views were shouted to incite violence and inflame the situation. There was serious disruption to the community and a substantial cost to the public purse.

The appellant's part was captured on CCTV and was part of an escalation shortly after 3 pm. He was part of a group of about 20 to 30 Asian males which ran several hundred yards from near Hanley Mosque to a car park where there were right wing protestors. Some members of his group, including the appellant himself, came armed with rocks, and one had a hammer. On arrival at the car park he was towards the front of the group and one of those who started to throw rocks and other projectiles at the opposing group, who at that time were not showing any violence. After his group had started to throw rocks and projectiles, some of the opposing group themselves threw projectiles back. The appellant himself can be seen in the CCTV footage to throw four rocks and then to retire and bend to the ground to collect more. He made efforts to break up a larger rock into pieces. That part of the confrontation and violence in which he was involved at the car park lasted a little under a minute before police in riot gear arrived and got between the rival groups. The appellant's group retired a little and after waiting for a while at the back of the group, he appeared to move off in the direction of the Mosque.

Others in the group stayed and moved forward again to confront the opposing group. By this time they were separated by the police in riot gear. Shortly after he had left, the appellant re-joined this group and he remained with it for the five minutes or so in which it continued to confront the police. During this time he was variously at the front or in the middle or at the back of the group of about 30 males. During this second period of his involvement, he had a white scarf wrapped across his face in an attempt to avoid detection.
This all took place in a busy town centre on a Saturday afternoon with members of the public present and in the area.
The appellant was aged 18 years and 3 months at the time of the offence. He had no previous convictions.

There was a pre-sentence report. The appellant claimed to the author that his involvement was reactive rather than premeditated and that he had been acting in self-defence. As the author recorded, this was inconsistent with the footage which clearly showed that the appellant had forearmed himself with rocks and was amongst the first to throw them from towards the front of the group before there was any violence from the opposing group. The author said that the behaviour observed in the footage "aligns with patterns of impulsivity and immaturity", and that "immaturity and limited capacity for weighing consequences, particularly in a charged group setting, were significant factors in the offending".

The author reported that the appellant had no family in the United Kingdom, having fled from Iran when he was 17 years of age, leaving his mother and siblings behind him. His father had been killed in Iran and he said that he had frequently witnessed violence perpetrated against the male members of his family. He had had no formal education in Iran.

At the sentencing hearing the judge indicated that he had prior to the hearing watched the CCTV footage. The judge said that although the prosecution note for sentencing said that the appellant had covered his face, he (the judge) had not been able to see that in the footage. Counsel for the Crown said that the officer in the case had identified some footage which did show that, but that she (counsel for the Crown) was not in a position to identify it for the court; and that she proposed to play only the footage of the first part of the incident. Mr Noble, who appeared for the defence then and has appeared before us, said to the sentencing judge that he was surprised by that aspect of the prosecution's note for sentence, because he had not himself seen any such covering of the face in the footage which he had watched. Counsel for the Crown then said that she would "concede the point". When the judge delivered his sentencing remarks he made no reference to such covering or indeed to the appellant's involvement in the second part of the confrontation, which was not part of the footage played in court. It is to be assumed that he sentenced on the basis of the first part only and without any reliance on any concealment to avoid detection, which is a statutory aggravating factor.
Looking at the footage, and without assistance, it is not easy to distinguish the appellant from others dressed in not dissimilar clothing during the second part of the incident.

In fact the appellant is the man with the white face covering participating in the second part of the incident shown in the footage. It was Mr Noble himself who drew this to the attention of the court in a letter a few days ago, having had the opportunity to be able to review the footage closely. He has apologised for not having been in a position to confirm that before the judge. In our view he is to be commended for fulfilling his duty to the court in drawing it to the court's attention and quite properly conceding the appellant's part in the second part of the incident.

The judge treated the offending as falling within category 1B of the Sentencing Council guideline for the offence, which has a starting point of three years' custody and a range of one to four years. There is no complaint about that categorisation. It was category 1 culpability, because there was a combination of four category 2 factors in the widespread disorder: there was serious disruption to the community; there was a substantial cost to the public purse; there were attacks on the police; and there was extensive damage to property. There was also some injury to members of the public.

intro.p: The judge treated as a seriously aggravating factor that the appellant was one of the people who threw rocks at the opposing group. The judge recognised that there were the following mitigating features:

content.p: the appellant's young age; he was only 18 at the time of the offence;
the absence of any previous convictions;
he difficulties in his family background, as described in the pre-sentence report; and
a positive character reference which came from his Social Services lead support worker who had been assigned when he had arrived as a 17 year old in this country.

The judge treated the aggravating and mitigating features as cancelling each other out. He said that the appropriate sentence after a trial would have been the category starting point of three years' custody. Applying a discount of 25 per cent for the guilty plea which was entered at the plea and trial preparation hearing, he determined that the sentence should be one of 27 months' imprisonment. The reference to imprisonment was a slip. It should have been to detention in a young offender institution. In fact, the sentence was correctly recorded as detention in a young offender institution. There is no need to correct the record and we need say no more about that aspect of the pronouncement in open court.

In submissions to us, which were attractively and concisely made, Mr Noble accepts that the judge correctly categorised the offending as category 1B, with a starting point of three years' custody, but submits that the mitigation significantly outweighed the aggravating features and accordingly that the appropriate sentence after a trial would have been significantly less than 32 months' custody, and therefore that after reduction for the guilty plea the sentence should be of a length which could have been and should be suspended.

intro.p: It is important to keep in mind the widespread national disorder which formed the context for this offending. Lady Carr CJ addressed the significance of that context in giving the judgment of the court in the conjoined appeals in R v Cush and Others [2024] EWCA Crim 1382; [2025] 1 Cr App R(S) 33. She said, amongst other things, this:

content.p: In late July and August 2024 a series of violent disturbances erupted across England, following a tragic incident on 29 July 2024, when three young girls were fatally stabbed at a dance class in Southport. The violence, fuelled by misinformation and far-right sentiment, spread to various towns and cities across the nation. Mosques and hotels housing asylum seekers were targeted. Significant damage was caused, and injuries were sustained. Those subjected to violence or threats of violence included police officers, whose duty it was to protect the communities under attack. Many of those responsible for the violence in England were quickly identified, arrested and brought before the courts, where they were swiftly convicted and sentenced.

In the context of widespread and significant public disorder, it is not only the precise individual acts of an offender that matter. It is the fact that the offender is taking part in violent disorder, threatening violence against other people and/or property, and is part and parcel of widespread threatening and alarming activity. That is the gravamen of the offending: being one of those who, by weight of numbers, pursues a common and unlawful purpose. Thus, whilst what an individual offender may have done themselves is of relevance, their acts must not be taken in isolation; rather the court must look at the whole picture.

intro.p: In Fox and Hicks [[2005] EWCA Crim 1122] the court at [16] encapsulated the principle in these terms:

content.p: 'In the case of public disorder it is important for the court to look at the whole picture, and although what an individual may have done by himself is of relevance, that is simply part of the whole to which he is contributing in his way, and the larger picture must be taken account of.'

In Blackshaw [[2011] EWCA Crim 2312] this court considered appeals against sentences imposed for offences committed in the summer of 2011 in a series of riots and incidents of serious disorder which began in London and spread to other parts of the country. The sentences under consideration had been imposed, not for offences contrary to the Public Order Act 1986, but rather for offences of burglary and theft committed during the disorder by persons looting shops. The court made clear that the context of the offending made the individual offences more serious than they would be if they stood in isolation, and justified sentences in excess of those which would be appropriate for offences of burglary and theft committed in different circumstances.

The weight to be given in the sentencing process to the need for deterrence may similarly vary according to the context of the offending. If public safety is under threat because of the potential spread of violence across the nation, then deterrence may be of the highest importance. The cases now before us illustrate the speed with which disorder in one part of the country may be replicated in other areas, each incident encouraging and promoting further incidents elsewhere. Defendants who choose to involve themselves in activity which threatens the safety and well-being of communities across the nation must therefore expect severe sentences designed not only to punish them but also to deter others. …

In cases such as those now before the court, a particular offence may properly be regarded as coming high in the range where one or more of the guideline factors is present to an unusually large or serious extent – for example, where the offender has participated in an incident which involves very widespread and/or particularly large scale acts of violence, and/or which contributes to a wider picture of incidents of disorder in different parts of the country. It may also come high in the range where the overall picture which the court must take into account makes it particularly important for the sentence not only to achieve appropriate punishment for the individual offender but also to deter others from engaging in similar disorder."

Although Cush was not cited to the judge or mentioned by him in his sentencing remarks, it was a widely publicised decision and is, in our view, likely to have been in the judge's mind when sentencing.

In this case the aggravating features required an uplift from the starting point to reflect that context and those principles, including the need for deterrence. In addition, there were serious aggravating features in the fact that the appellant had sought the confrontation by travelling some distance in a group armed with projectiles and in one case a hammer. The appellant himself was armed with rocks and he had been in the forefront of starting this aspect of the violence by repeatedly throwing rocks. An uplift from the starting point to somewhere close to the top of the category range was required to reflect those considerations.

Mr Noble has urged upon us the weight to be attached to the various aspects of personal mitigation which the judge mentioned. They were indeed significant. Mr Noble suggested that because of the appellant's young age and because, he submitted, of the references which we have mentioned in the pre-sentence report to immaturity, that he could properly be treated as if he were under 18 at the time and afforded as much as one third discount on grounds of age alone.

We are unable to accept that submission. What was said in the pre-sentence report was not that the appellant was immature for his age, but simply that the behaviour exhibited signs of immaturity. He was of course entitled to significant mitigation for the fact that he was only 18 and, as is well recognised now, turning 18 does not involve a cliff edge. Young people do not fully develop into maturity until some time in their early to mid-twenties.

However, taking all the personal mitigation together, it was not, in our view, of sufficient weight that a sentence after trial of three years' custody can be said to be manifestly excessive in the light of the aggravating features which we have identified. That is all the more so taking into account the fact, which was not apparent to the judge when sentencing, that the appellant's involvement was not limited to the period of about one minute in the first part of the incident surrounding his throwing of the rocks, but extended to the second part of the confrontation when for about five minutes he was disguised by a face covering and was participating in the further confrontation. However, we make clear that the commendable fulfilment of his duty to the court by Mr Noble in drawing that to our attention has not been determinative of our conclusion.
For these reasons the appeal against sentence will be dismissed.
